title: The Waiting Room Is the Most Honest Building in Town
body: Nobody chooses to be in a waiting room. That is what makes it interesting. Every other public space is full of people performing some version of themselves, but a waiting room collects people who have surrendered. The appointment set the time, the queue set the order, and the only remaining freedom is where to sit. Watch a room like that for twenty minutes and you learn things about people that no interview would tell you. The person who arrived early and took the seat facing the door. The one who paces the corridor every four minutes, checking a clock that has not moved since the last check. The couple who divide a single phone between them, one earbud each, sharing something small while the world waits. There is a strange equality to it. The coat rack does not care which coat belongs to whom. The plastic chairs were purchased by the dozen, and everyone gets the same one. Status walks in with you, and then it has nowhere to sit, so it ends up holding the same outdated magazine as everybody else. I have started thinking of these rooms as the most honest buildings in town. They record what people actually do when nothing can be done. Some sleep upright with their mouth slightly open. Some talk to strangers and discover, briefly, that talking to strangers is fine. Some fold and unfold the same paper form until it has the texture of cloth. The nervous ones rehearse what they plan to say, lips moving without sound, and the rehearsed sentence always comes out different, and always comes out fine. The clocks deserve their own paragraph. There is always at least one, and it is always slightly wrong. Everyone in the room knows it is wrong, and everyone uses it anyway, because a wrong clock you can see beats a right clock you cannot. Time in a waiting room is not measured in minutes. It is measured in how many people entered the inner door before you, in how many pages of a magazine count as polite, in how long it takes a child to ask, loudly, if it is almost over. What fascinates me most is how the room changes people after their turn. The ones who go in come out different, and the room reads the difference instantly. Some come out lighter, some heavier, some rehearsing new sentences for a different conversation. Nobody claps, nobody asks. The chairs rotate one position, and the room absorbs the news without a word. I have decided to stop treating these hours as lost time, and to start treating them as the only hours when a certain kind of seeing is possible. Phones gave us the ability to leave a room without leaving it, and I took that deal for years. But the room is where the people are. The room is where a stranger's coat reminds you of your father's, where the wrong clock is somehow the most reliable thing in the building, where everyone agrees, without ever saying it, that today it is our turn to wait. The queue will get to all of us eventually. It already got the person whose chair is still warm. All that remains of the choice is what to notice while it happens. When you are next stuck in one of these rooms, no phone, no screen, nothing to optimize. What will your eyes actually do with the twenty minutes?
